sources.note: For ALEKANO, not Tokano: p. 3 'There are several degrees of stress conditioned by tone. Greatest stress is on a high tone syllable followed by a low tone in the same word. Lesser stress is on a final high tone preceded by a low tone syllable. In a word containing two syllables with the same tone, the first has light stress. Alekano has two phonemic tones.' Not transferable to Tokano without a Tokano source.

sources.note: For DANO, not Tokano: two tones, stress non-phonemic, 'Stress falls on the first high tone in a word; otherwise on the second low tone' (p. 2). Cited only to show the family pattern; not a Tokano statement.

sources.note: Names 'the three languages in the northwest end of the Goroka Valley as Alekano, Tokano, and Dano' (p. 2) -- confirms Tokano is treated as a separate language, not an Alekano dialect; explains that in published Alekano materials the acute accent marks glottal closure and 'no indication of tone is given' (pp. 1-2, 4). Nothing on Tokano stress.
